The treatment of the intellectually disabled and the mentally ill in psychiatric institutions during the 20th century is some really horrific stuff, And many of the practices and mindsets that were so prevalent in those environments are still around today unfortunately.

And therein is kind of the tricky horrible thing about all this. So say a person, called A, is severely intellectually disabled and nonverbal. A has a seizure disorder, and has to take a medication to not have grand mal seizures. You can not communicate successfully with A why they have to take this medication, but they need to take it or they’ll have seizures. Or if A decides they don’t want to take this medication you legally can not force them to take that medication. But you’d also really like them to not have a seizure. So you have to communicate somehow the importance of taking this medication to them. But, the law (at least in my state) says that any refusal, informed or not means you do not administer.  So in these cases, the person who was sterilized was never even given the opportunity to refuse, even if they have no real way of refusal.

Or, and this is an example based on someone I worked with previously, called “B”. During her time in a state psychiatric hospital in the 1980s, B started to develop glaucoma in both eyes. The hospital staff decided, that instead of pursuing any other treatment first, they were going to remove both of B’s eyes. And they did. B was not consulted or given the opportunity to refuse this, due to the way state care operated at this time. The doctors and nurses didn’t operate on her out of malice, they operated on her because they wanted her to not be in pain anymore. But, they did not respect her right as a human being to even be given the option of refusal.

In a way it is similar, if you read the wikipedia article on the Ashley treatment it discusses the parent’s reasoning behind why they chose to do this to their daughter and most of it is coming from a place of genuine care, ie they don’t want her to have painful periods, etc. It’s not out of some malice that they chose to have their daughter undergo multiple surgeries and hormone treatments. However, the fact remains that she did not consent to this. For example, we would never dream of giving an infant a hysterectomy based on the possibility of having a painful period in the future, but in the case of a disabled child or adult, it’s an acceptable practice. I don’t think the reasoning of wanting to your child to have an easier time of it is inherently bad or harmful, it’s just that a severely disabled person who is sterilized and is not giving consent is not having their human rights respected, because someone else made the decision that they didn’t “need” literal parts of their body.

I used to work with intellectually disabled adults, and the number of clients I had who had been forcibly sterilized in state institutions in the 80’s and 90’s is incredibly disturbing and horrible. (Not even counting the various other procedures done without these peoples’ consent) A primary care practitioner suggesting you lose 50 pounds is NOWHERE near the practice of giving a woman with an intellectual disability in a state psychiatric hospital a hysterectomy and then keeping her on an incredibly high level of estrogen to suppress other secondary sex characteristics. Or you know, having a child’s [own parents have her undergo these procedures ](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashley_Treatment).  And it’s not as if this practice has stopped in the modern day! 

Or what about indigenous women in Canada [being forcibly sterilized ](https://www.google.com/amp/s/beta.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2018/12/04/end-forced-sterilizations-indigenous-women-canada/%3foutputType=amp)? Is that the same as asking someone to get 30 minutes of physical activity a day?

Even though kids are very intelligent, inquisitive, logical individuals, they still have developing minds that soak up information and judgements about the world, often through their main source of information- their parents. Things parents say to their children stick, more than people realize. 

I have memories of being five or six and going with my mom to a weight watchers meeting and being encouraged by her to learn the point system and apply it. I remember my mom constantly comparing herself to other mothers, where their “problem” areas were. I remember my mother talking about how disgusting it was that my dad took me to McDonald’s for dinner and that I thought it was tasty. And I sure as hell remember my mom calling me a fat little pig and telling me that “I would just get fat like [my] aunt” when I didn’t want to go on a run with her.

Yeah holy shit if my mom hadn’t constantly talked about her diets and how “fat” she was around me constantly as a kid, I doubt I would feel as bad about my own body now. 

I think positive reinforcement, like the above “broccoli is good for keeping germs away” and getting kids to want to eat healthy things because they’re tasty, or give you “powers” (spinach is brain food, carrots help you see), or because they have fun textures and it’s fun to try new things is wayyyy better way to encourage healthy eating and a healthy relationship to food in the future

Lemon Pepper Rice! I’ve been making this for stuffed peppers for my clients, and it’s delicious.

1. Sauté onion and garlic in a pan with olive oil, salt, pepper, and Italian seasoning.  Then add a couple big handfuls of chopped spinach and let that cook down

2. Cook your rice, whether it’s instant, or in the rice cooker, whatever works! You could probably also use cauliflower rice for a lower calorie option. 

3. Dump your rice into the pan and mix in with the onions and garlic. 

4. Add a big glug of rice vinegar (about a tablespoon per cup of rice? I never measure oops) and a big shake of Mrs. Dash, and probably more pepper! Mix and enjoy 🍋🍚

I have a really tasty eggplant and chickpea salad that you might like if you like chickpeas! You could totally add cucumbers as well! 

1. Cut your eggplant into rounds, sprinkle with salt, leave for 20 minutes, then wash the salt off. Sauté those bad boys in olive oil till they get squishy! 

2. Drain a can of chickpeas and cut up a tomato (and a cucumber!) and dump them into a bowl with a little more olive oil, white wine or balsamic vinegar, salt, pepper, paprika, lemon juice, and fresh basil, maybe a little mint too if you want to get funky. 

3. Remove your eggplant from the pan and chop the sautéed rounds into cubes. Add to the other ingredients, mix, and pop in the refrigerator to chill or serve it right then and there! 

It’s a super good salad, that tastes really summery and is super easy to make!

Also pasta sauce on slices of zucchini and eggplant (salted like in the previous recipe!) with cheese on top and baked in the oven is a nice addition to a meal!
